reading.rtitle: The Question That Was Not About Five Years
paras: When Marina Toledo sat down with her board in 2023, the chair asked her the question every founder is asked and almost none prepare for: what would this company look like in five years? “I gave the answer I had given a hundred times,” she says. “Bigger. More clients. More countries. It took me two years to understand that he was not asking about the company at all. He was asking whether I had ever seriously imagined a version of it that I had not already chosen.”

So she went back and did the exercise properly. She wrote three futures, one page each. In the first, the company doubled down on the vertical it already owned: no new markets, every last cent of profit reinvested in the product, headcount flat for two years. In the second, it opened two offices abroad, which meant raising money, which meant dilution — her stake would fall from seventy-one percent to somewhere near forty. In the third, it spun off the analytics unit as an independent business and sold the rest.

“The pages were useful,” she says, “but the sentence that changed the conversation was much smaller. Every line on those pages started with if. If we raised, we would lose control of the timetable. If we stayed exactly where we are, we would have a shorter runway than anybody on that board believed. Once you write it that way, nobody argues about whether the future is good. They argue about the trade-off, and a trade-off is something a board can actually decide.”

What surprised her most was the third page. Selling the core and keeping the analytics unit was the option nobody had proposed, including her, and on paper it was the weakest of the three. But writing it forced her to say out loud what the company’s real moat was. “I had always assumed it was the client list. When I described the version where we sold the client list and kept the twelve engineers, I could see that I would still have a company. When I described the reverse, I would not. That told me more about the business than any of the numbers did.”

She is careful about what the exercise is for. “It is not a plan. Three pages of hypotheticals will not tell you what to do next quarter. What they do is stop you defending the future you already picked. If somebody asks me that question today, I do not describe one future. I describe the trade I would be making in each of them, and then I ask them which trade they would take. That is a conversation. The other thing was a speech.”
reading.source: A composite portrait of a founder-led board conversation, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how a board decides whether a company should raise money abroad.
To show that the value of the five-year question is not the answer but the trade-off each future forces you to name -- and that writing them as conditionals is what lets a board decide.
To argue that spinning off part of a company is usually the strongest option.

listenings.text: I ask every founder the same question in the first meeting, and I am not looking for a forecast. Nobody in this business believes a five-year forecast, including the person presenting it. What I am listening for is whether this is a person who has ever seriously considered a company other than the one he already decided to build. When the answer comes back as bigger, more clients, more countries, I stop listening, because that is not a future. That is the same company with larger numbers on it, and it tells me the founder has never once sat down and imagined losing something. What I want is two versions, and the trade-off between them. Tell me the one where you keep control and grow slowly, tell me the one where you take money and move fast, tell me what you would give up in each, and then tell me which one you would take and why. A founder who can do that in four minutes is a founder I can work with for eight years.

Founders count the wrong number. They watch the percentage, because the percentage is on the page in front of them, and they stop counting the thing that actually changes, which is how many decisions they can still make alone. I raised at the end of my fourth year. I still owned a majority afterwards, comfortably, and by the middle of the second year after that round I was explaining a single hiring decision to three people before I made it. Nobody blocked me. Nobody had to. The explaining is the cost, and the explaining does not show up anywhere in the ownership table. If I were doing it again, I would do exactly one thing differently. I would write down, before the money arrived, which decisions I wanted to keep for myself. Not the big ones, because everybody protects the big ones. The ordinary ones. Because after the round, the ordinary decisions are the ones that quietly stop being yours, and by the time you notice, the habit is already built.

extra_audio.text: Let me give you two versions, not one. In the first, we reinvest everything and headcount grows slowly. In the second, we raise, and the dilution would take me close to forty percent. So the trade-off is the same in both: speed or control. If I had to choose today, I would take the second one. And now I would like to hear which one you would take.
